title: Viking Lifting Wisdom
summary: Part of his 'lifting wisdom' series: NH explores Viking warrior culture, physiques, mythology, gender roles and Old Norse philosophy, arguing that a culture which ranks men by strength produces strong men and healthy societies. He contrasts it with modern Western culture, which he says rewards weakness, and urges men to reclaim values that promote their own strength.
claims: Viking imagery is common in lifting culture (shirts, tattoos, hardcore gym emblems) because Vikings are the modern archetype of masculinity and power
In a warrior culture only the strong are valued, so every man strives to be as strong as possible; a weak man who cannot defend his family ranks low in the hierarchy
A warrior culture creates strong men while a weak culture creates 'cultural warriors' who bicker online about politics and pop culture
Average Viking men were only 5'6-5'8 (women 5'3-5'5), but warrior burial sites hold men of 6'0-6'4; the gap is selection bias since only the tallest and strongest were sent to fight
Vikings of all heights were described as far more muscular than the average European, largely thanks to a dairy-heavy, high-protein, high-calorie diet

Vikings built muscle through physical labour (farming, carrying loads, rowing, shipbuilding, chopping wood) rather than weights; physical work builds muscle anywhere and the gym is simply the most optimal environment
Rowing and wood chopping alone train the whole body; daily heavy labour plus plenty of protein and calories made every Viking man jacked compared with the rest of the population
Vikings fought with axes and little armour, which required exceptional strength; they relied on surprise raids and deliberately cultivated a fearsome reputation so enemies would not fight back

The Berserkers (bear-skin wearing Odin worshippers who entered battle trances) inspired Berserk's Guts and the Apostle troop, and may lie behind European werewolf myths; even Vikings viewed them as villains
Vikings bathed weekly, combed their hair daily and smelled good; English chroniclers complained they seduced local wives, showing grooming plus muscle beat the competition
Norse and other Indo-European gods are idealised, muscular, human-like role models men can relate to, unlike the distant god of monotheism
Valhalla only admits those who die in battle and is spent feasting and wrestling daily; what a culture believes is paradise dictates how its people live
Norse philosophy valued loyalty, modesty and compassion but placed self-reliance and strength first: the loyalty, modesty and compassion of the weak are useless
Vikings wanted strong individuals because only strong individuals make a strong collective; strength was a prerequisite to being useful to the group
To get on an Icelandic fishing boat you had to lift natural stones: ~50 lb = useless, 100 lb = weakling, ~200 lb = half strong, ~340 lb (155-160 kg) = full strong
A natural stone is much harder to lift than the same weight on a barbell; most commercial gym members could not pick up the 200 lb stone

Viking boys had to pass rites of passage (survive 15 winters, ride a horse, learn hunting, fishing, building) to become men; modern society has lost rites of passage like military service, so men stay boys
Women in Viking society selected men on strength and ability to provide; if modern women did the same, men would be forced to improve
Viking society was meritocratic: freedom had to be earned through strength, and women who could fight (shield-maidens) were free to do so
Viking women held power indirectly: they ran family finances and pushed men and boys toward masculinity, raids and vengeance
Old Norse wisdom: wealth is temporary but wisdom is eternal; travel was encouraged because wisdom comes only from experience
Vikings believed in fate yet were optimistic and courageous, showing determinism need not produce weak men if the associated values are healthy
A Viking knew his family and community would suffer if he failed; modern men lack that weight of responsibility
Legendary Icelandic feats: shepherds carrying a 400 lb stone around a sheep pen, fishermen lifting stones of hundreds of pounds for bragging rights
Modern Western values encourage weakness; people equate absence of rules with freedom, but rules are guides and strong structures produce strong individuals
He does not advocate becoming Vikings again but reclaiming ancient wisdom: always turn toward things that promote your own strength, because that is where virtue lies
